intro: Both ている and てある can describe a state that is left over after a change: the window is open, the light is on, the name is written on the board. The difference is whether a person is behind it. Intransitive verb + ている simply reports the state (窓が開いている, the window is open). Transitive verb + てある reports a state that someone created on purpose and left that way (窓が開けてある, the window has been opened, someone left it open). In both, the thing is normally marked with が.

skills.rule: State with no one in view: X が + intransitive-ている. State someone set up on purpose: X が + transitive-てある. Someone doing it now: X を + transitive-ている.
skills.explain:
With a verb of change, ている does not mean 'is doing'; it means 'has changed and stays changed'. 窓が開いている is 'the window is open', not 'the window is opening'. 電気がついている: the light is on. 財布が落ちている: there is a wallet lying on the ground.

てある attaches only to transitive verbs and adds a purpose: someone did this and left the result for a reason. 窓が開けてある (aired on purpose), 黒板に予定が書いてある, ビールが冷やしてある (ready for the party). The doer is left unsaid. Use it for preparations and notices. X を + てある (窓を開けてある) also occurs and stresses the preparation; が is the default.

A transitive verb with ている is an ordinary action in progress or a habit, with the doer as subject and the object with を: 兄が窓を開けている (my brother is opening the window). ておく is also an action: 'do it in advance', 窓を開けておきます. Neither ている nor ておく describes a leftover state of the window itself.
patterns: X が [intransitive]-ている → X is in that state
X が [transitive]-てある → X has been put in that state on purpose
人 が X を [transitive]-ている → someone is doing it now
人 が X を [transitive]-ておく → someone does it in advance

examples.jp: 窓[まど]が{開[あ]いています}。
部屋[へや]の電気[でんき]が{ついています}。
examples.en: The light in the room is on.

examples.jp: 窓[まど]が{開[あ]けてあります}。
examples.en: The window has been left open (someone opened it on purpose).

examples.jp: 黒板[こくばん]に今日[きょう]の予定[よてい]が{書[か]いてあります}。
examples.en: Today's schedule is written on the blackboard.

examples.jp: パーティーのビールはもう{冷[ひ]やしてあります}。
examples.en: The beer for the party has already been chilled.

examples.jp: 兄[あに]は今[いま]、窓[まど]を{開[あ]けています}。
examples.en: My brother is opening the window right now.

contrast.note: 窓が開いている reports what you see. Use it when nobody's intention matters, or when you do not know how it happened.
窓を開けておきました is an action report: 'I opened it in advance'. 窓が開けてあります describes the result someone can see now. Different particle (を vs が) and different subject.
窓を開けている is an action in progress with a doer. It never means 'the window is open'.

mistakes.bad: 窓[まど]が{開[あ]けています}。
mistakes.good: 窓[まど]が{開[あ]いています}。
mistakes.note: With が and no doer, a transitive verb + ている makes no sense. Use the intransitive for the state.

mistakes.bad: ドアが{閉[し]まってあります}。
mistakes.good: ドアが{閉[し]めてあります}。
mistakes.note: てある takes only transitive verbs. Or say ドアが閉まっています for the plain state.

mistakes.bad: 道[みち]に財布[さいふ]が{落[お]としてあります}。
mistakes.good: 道[みち]に財布[さいふ]が{落[お]ちています}。
mistakes.note: 落としてある would mean someone dropped it there on purpose. A wallet lying in the road is 落ちている.

skills.tip: Ask 'did someone set this up on purpose?' Yes: transitive + てある. No, or don't know: intransitive + ている. Both with が.
